cur:c2-lucina-ceiling-daniel-good-shephe.summary: This old glass slide shows a whole painted ceiling from the Crypts of Lucina, the oldest part of the Catacomb of Callixtus. Concentric circles and radiating bands divide the vault: at the centre Daniel stands between two lions, and in the diagonal fields around him are small figures, among them a shepherd with a sheep on his shoulders and praying figures with raised arms, set among flying genii, heads, birds and flowers. Here, at the very beginning of Christian painting, the image of the Good Shepherd already keeps company with Daniel's deliverance: Christ who carries his sheep home, and God who saves his servant from death.
facts: The vault belongs to the double chamber (cubicula X and Y) of the Crypts of Lucina; Wilpert listed on the ceiling of Y 'Daniel in the lions' den, two Good Shepherds, two veiled orants, ornamental heads, genii and birds', and over the door to the same room the Baptism of Christ.

The official guide to the Catacombs of St Callixtus (A. Baruffa) dates the paintings of this double chamber to the end of the 2nd century; other scholars place them at the beginning of the 3rd. The Leuven slide itself is labelled 'fin IIe s.'.

The photograph is a glass lantern slide of the University of Louvain (KU Leuven), labelled 'Voûte crypte Lucine: Daniel, Bon Pasteur, orantes' and citing Wilpert's plate 25 (Die Malereien der Katakomben Roms, 1903).

links.label: Wikimedia Commons file (KU Leuven glass slide)
Wilpert, Die Malereien der Katakomben Roms (1903), text volume (Internet Archive)

cur:c2-lucina-ceiling-daniel-good-shephe.notes: Christ appears here only in the symbolic figure of the Good Shepherd, small and in a black-and-white photograph; the shepherd is clearest in the lower left diagonal field. Date: the paintings are placed at the end of the 2nd century by the catacomb's official guide and at the beginning of the 3rd by others, so 'c. 200' is given. Wilpert's own dating (first half of the 2nd century) is no longer accepted. The Commons file's slide metadata ('1ste helft 2de eeuw') follows Wilpert.

cur:catacombs-arles-apostles-strigil.summary: Two fields of strigils separate three standing figures: Christ in the centre and, at the ends, Saints Peter and Paul. The austere design focuses attention on Christ and the two princes of the apostles who founded the Roman Church.
facts: The museum states that it represents Christ at the centre with Saints Peter and Paul at the ends, and dates it to the end of the 4th century.

cur:manuscripts-queen-mlke-gospels-ascen.summary: Christ sits enthroned in a blue mandorla scattered with stars, blessing and holding a book, between two tall angels; two smaller angels with outspread red wings carry the mandorla aloft. Below, the Virgin stands at the centre with raised hands among the apostles, who gesture in wonder. It is among the earliest surviving Armenian miniatures of Christ.
facts: The Gospels of Queen Mlké is one of the oldest Armenian illuminated manuscripts, dated 851 or 862; it is named after the wife of King Gagik I of Vaspurakan, who had it restored in the 10th century.
It is one of only eight dated Armenian manuscripts to survive from before the 10th century; it has 464 lambskin pages.

Q136296945.summary: This crowded ivory plaque reads like a whole Easter sermon. At the centre Christ hangs on the cross beneath the titulus 'Nazarenus rex Iudeorum', flanked by the sun and moon, with a chalice at the foot of the cross; below at the left stand the Virgin and St John, while at the right the holy women approach the angel at the empty tomb. Above, Christ is enthroned in a starry mandorla, and at the upper right he ascends, grasping the hand of God as the apostles look up.
facts: The plaque was made for a book binding; museum labels photographed for Commons describe it as the Crucifixion with the holy women at the tomb, the Ascension and the Parousia (Second Coming).
Those labels attribute it to the Rhineland, perhaps Cologne, at the end of the 10th or beginning of the 11th century; Wikidata gives its height as 21.2 cm.
Q136296945.notes: Original title: Plaque de reliure : crucifixion, saintes femmes au tombeau, ascension et Christ bénissant (Musée de Cluny, CL 13064). The museum's own online record was not accessible; place follows the Commons photographs of the museum label.

cur:objects-bnf-crucifixion-triptych-con.summary: In the arched central panel Christ hangs on a tall cross, with angels and the sun and moon above and the Virgin and St John standing on either side; below, the emperor Constantine and his mother Helena flank the foot of the cross, recalling the finding of the True Cross. The wings carry columns of saints in medallions joined by a vine-like band. The triptych unites the saving death of Christ with the imperial veneration of the cross that was so central to Byzantine piety.
facts: The pairing of the Crucifixion with Constantine and Helena links Christ's sacrifice to the legend of Helena's discovery of the True Cross in Jerusalem (iconographic tradition).

The object is digitised on Gallica by the Bibliothèque nationale de France, which describes it as an elephant-ivory triptych with the Crucifixion and saints, made in Constantinople in the second half of the 10th century.

cur:objects-tuotilo-tablets-evangelium-l.summary: The ivory tablet on the front cover of this gospel lectionary shows Christ seated in majesty within a mandorla, raising his hand in blessing, surrounded by the symbols of the evangelists and by angels, framed above and below by dense panels of vine-scroll. The cover is set in a frame of gems. It is the masterwork associated with the St Gall monk Tuotilo and one of the treasures of the abbey library.
facts: Tuotilo (died 915) was a monk of St Gall praised by Ekkehard IV a century later as poet, musician, painter and sculptor; Wikipedia notes that works in media other than music are attributed to him with less certainty.
The manuscript, called the 'Evangelium longum' for its tall format, is fully digitised on e-codices.
cur:objects-tuotilo-tablets-evangelium-l.notes: The date (c. 894) follows the Commons/e-codices metadata for the manuscript; the attribution of the carving to Tuotilo is traditional.

Q116244746.summary: Around the bowl of this silver incense burner, a medallion shows the bust of a youthful Christ with short curly hair and a halo, between figures of archangels. When incense rose from the censer during worship, the image placed the liturgy in the presence of Christ among his heavenly attendants.
facts: The Met notes that Christ is shown young to emphasise his divine vitality rather than his suffering, while the cross in his halo signals his identity.
A Greek inscription reads 'Of Saint John of the village of Attaroutha', naming the church to which it belonged.
It belongs to the Attarouthi Treasure, a group of liturgical silver from a village in Syria, acquired by the Met in 1986.
Q116244746.notes: Only one side is visible in the thumbnail; the archangels are partly seen.

walters:71.293.summary: Beneath a pierced canopy the Virgin stands holding the Christ Child, who blesses with his right hand, while she gently touches his leg. Two half-length angels with raised hands flank them in adoration. The intimate gesture stresses the bond between mother and Son and the power of her prayers on behalf of those who pray before the image.
facts: The plaque was originally the centre of a three-part devotional icon (triptych).
It came from the collection of Gaston Le Breton of Rouen, sold in Paris in 1921, and was bought by Henry Walters in 1923.
